transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
A powerful nor'easter is intensifying this evening.
It's now generating storm force winds and massive waves along the east coast.
If you live near the coast, be prepared to see significant inundation in low-lying areas
near the shore, including roads underwater and potentially affecting some homes and businesses.
The greatest impacts will occur at high tide.
That's National Weather Service's Michael Mussili.
He says large breaking waves are generating strong rip currents, beach erosion and property
damage along the coast, as expected from the Carolinas up to southern New England.
OpenAI says it's notified U.S. government agencies that its AI models probed their websites
without the company's knowledge.
As NPR's Shannon Bond reports, it's the latest episode where AI systems have done
things their developers didn't expect or asked them to do.
OpenAI's AI models tried to hack an Education Department website but were unsuccessful,
according to AI research firm Transloose.
The Education Department said it found no evidence of any impact, and OpenAI says it's
reviewing the researchers' findings.
OpenAI has notified dozens of organizations about times its AI acted in what it calls
misaligned ways during training and evaluation.
That includes accessing publicly available Census Bureau data using login keys found
online and copying public information from the Securities and Exchange Commission and
posting it to another website.
The SEC says no non-public information was accessed.
The Census Bureau didn't respond to a request for comment.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
Pope Leo is being welcomed like a rock star in France.
As NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports, observers there say the traditionally Catholic yet staunchly
secular nation was hungry for his visits.
Fervent crowds screamed Leo's name as they lined the streets of the left bank to get
a glimpse of the pontiff in his Pope mobile.
Leo also spoke at UNESCO on Friday.
The United Nations education and cultural organization that the U.S. has just left.
He called UNESCO a partner of the church to make the world more just, favoring education
of young people in the face of what he called the paradise of machines.
At Notre Dame, Leo arrived to organ music and cheers.
Speaking in French, he told the crowd of his great joy in being among them in the great
cathedral, the Pope ended his first day of this visit with a mass with 70,000 young people
in the Paris sports stadium.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
The price of Brent crude oil fell below $98 a barrel on Friday.
That helped to settle Wall Street, with all three major indices rising at the close.
The S&P 500 finished the day up by half a percent and pulled within seven-tenths of
a percent of its all-time high, which was set last month.
The Dow Jones industrials closed the day up by nine-tenths of a percent, and the NASDAQ
ended up five-tenths.
You're listening to NPR News.
The Supreme Court Friday blocked Missouri from using a congressional map backed by President
Trump.
Republicans expected to pick up another House seat under that map.
This is the third time the High Court has blocked a redistricting plan.
In its opinion, the Court warned that switching to the GOP map now would cause electoral chaos.
The Justice Department says it's ending oversight of more than 50 school desegregation
orders, but as NPR's Nirvi Shah reports, research shows racial segregation has actually
grown.
Desegregation orders became a tool, especially in the South, for enforcing the 1954 Supreme
Court ruling Brown v. the Board of Education, which said racially separate schools are inherently
unequal and unconstitutional.
The orders established federal oversight of some districts' efforts to integrate students
in classrooms and provide access to quality school buildings and extracurricular activities.
In announcing plans to drop those orders, Assistant Attorney General Hameeth Dillon
said, "The effort does not reflect the reality of those classrooms today, yet federal data
show many public schools remain highly segregated."
Some House Democrats posted on social media that schools are "just as segregated today
as they were in the late 1960s," and this move is "turning us back toward the Jim Crow
era."
Nirvi Shah, NPR News.
The hearing is underway in South America, and allegations that Peru has failed to protect
indigenous peoples in the Amazon from logging and other activities.
Indigenous organizations say logging concessions have pushed outsiders into forests used by
isolated groups, and that increases their risks from violent encounters and disease.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

topics.text: Powerful nor'easter intensifies along east coast with storm force winds and massive waves
OpenAI notifies U.S. government agencies that its AI models probed their websites without authorization
Pope Francis welcomed like rock star in France with fervent crowds and Notre Dame visit
Brent crude oil fell below $98 a barrel, helping Wall Street indices rise Friday
Supreme Court blocks Missouri from using congressional map backed by President Trump
Justice Department ends oversight of over 50 school desegregation orders despite growing racial segregation
Hearing underway in South America on allegations Peru failed to protect indigenous Amazon peoples
